h1: Wine pricing and restaurant mark-ups in India, explained
title: Wine Prices and Mark-ups in India | Craft Beer School
desc: Why a bottle of wine costs what it does in India, from winery cost and excise to retail margins and restaurant mark-ups.
teaser: The same bottle can cost three times as much in a restaurant as in a shop. Here is where every rupee goes.
standfirst: Wine in India passes through a winery, a state excise system, a distributor and a retailer before it reaches your glass. In a restaurant it picks up another mark-up on top. Knowing how the price is built helps you spot fair value on a list.
sections: Why wine costs more than you expect

Wine is made once a year from one harvest. The grapes, the tanks and the barrels sit idle for most of the year while the wine waits to be sold. A winery's cost per bottle carries all of that time and capital, which is why even a modest wine is not cheap to make.

Then the state takes its share. In India alcohol is a state subject, so every state sets its own excise duties, fees and taxes. The same wine can carry very different duty in two neighbouring states. Some states have supported their own wine industries with lighter duties on locally made wine, while others tax wine much like spirits. Rules change, so the only reliable figure is the current notification for that state.
How a shelf price is built

Follow one bottle of Indian wine from winery to shop:

  1. Winery cost. Grapes, fermentation, ageing, bottle, cork or screwcap, label and carton.
  2. Winery margin. What keeps the winery in business.
  3. State levies. Excise duty, licence and label registration costs plus any other fees the state charges, sometimes on volume and sometimes on price.
  4. Distributor margin. For warehousing, delivery, credit and sales calls. In some states a state corporation is the wholesaler.
  5. Retailer margin. The shop's cut.
  6. The final price. Many states fix a maximum retail price, so you should see the same price in every shop in that state.

Imported wine adds customs duty and shipping before any of this starts, which is why an everyday European wine can cost several times more in India than in its home country. Our guide on excise for finance teams explains how these duties are worked out.

Restaurants rarely sell a bottle at the shop price. A common rule of thumb worldwide is that a wine list sits at around two to three times the retail price, with higher mark-ups on the cheapest bottles and lower ones at the top of the list. Indian restaurants often follow a similar pattern, though there is no fixed standard and it varies hugely by city and venue.

The mark-up pays for more than the liquid. The restaurant has its own bar licence, which can be expensive. It holds stock for months, buys glassware that breaks, trains staff and gives you a table, service and a corkscrew. A fair list will show that thinking. A bad one marks up the cheapest wine five times because it knows people order the second cheapest bottle.
Why a glass costs so much

A standard 750 ml bottle gives five 150 ml glasses. Restaurants price a glass so that the first two or three glasses cover the bottle, because once a bottle is opened the clock starts.

Oxygen begins to flatten wine within a day or two, faster in a warm room. A white left on the back bar in an Indian summer may be past its best by the next evening. Sparkling wine loses its fizz. A venue that pours wine by the glass is also paying for the bottles that never finish. Some use preservation systems that blanket an opened bottle with inert gas, which lets them offer better wines by the glass.
How to find value on a wine list

• Look at the middle of the list. The percentage mark-up is often kinder there than on the cheapest bottle.
  • Try Indian wine. It carries no import duty, so a good Indian wine often gives more quality for the money than an imported bottle at the same price.
  • Ask what is open. A wine already open for glasses may be offered at a good price.
  • Ask about corkage. Some restaurants let you bring your own bottle for a fee, where state rules and the venue's licence allow. Check before you arrive.
  • Ignore the bottle price as a quality signal. Ask what the staff enjoy and why.
What this means for a winery

If you are on the other side of the list, pricing decides whether a wine ever gets ordered. Work back from the price a guest will accept on a menu in your target city, take off the restaurant's mark-up, the distributor and the duty. See what is left for you. Many small wineries find that the price they need and the price the market will pay are far apart. The same logic is behind why craft beer costs more than mass lager.

Building that pricing ladder for each state is one of the hardest parts of running a winery. It is easy to get wrong when you only see your own costs.
faqs: Why is imported wine so expensive in India?
Imported wine pays customs duty on arrival as well as state excise, distributor and retail margins. Each layer is calculated on a price that already includes the one before.
Is a restaurant wine mark-up of three times normal?
It is common worldwide for a list to sit around two to three times retail, with bigger mark-ups on cheap bottles. There is no fixed standard in India and it varies by venue.
Why does wine cost different amounts in different states?
Alcohol is a state subject in India, so each state sets its own duties, fees and price rules. Check the current state notification for exact figures.
Can I take my own wine to a restaurant in India?
Some restaurants allow it for a corkage fee where their licence and state rules permit. Always ask the venue first.
